Chapter 9: The Limits of Compensation—Can Good Make Up for Harm?
You know, there’s this comforting idea a lot of us hold onto—the thought that the joys in life can somehow make up for the pain we go through. Maybe you’ve heard people say that love, achievement, or those little bursts of happiness can balance out the tough times. It’s a hope that the good moments are enough to justify all the bad ones.
But when we stop and ask ourselves whether bringing someone new into the world is the right thing to do, that way of thinking starts to unravel a bit.
Picture a man who’s been through his share of hardships—illness, loss, disappointment. He’s felt real pain. But he’s also had moments of pure joy—the warmth of a close friend’s hug, the pride after finishing something meaningful, or just sitting quietly, watching a sunset. Like many of us, he tries to weigh the good against the bad, hoping those sweet moments can somehow make up for the suffering he’s endured.
But here’s the thing—compensation is not the same as prevention. Having happiness later on doesn’t erase the pain that already happened. It doesn’t make it disappear. The suffering is still there, a part of his story, no matter how much joy comes afterward.
For someone who’s already here, it makes sense to chase happiness, to look for meaning in the struggles, and to hope tomorrow might be better. That’s part of being human. But when we’re talking about creating a new life, the question changes. The harm and suffering—those are guaranteed to show up at some point. But the joys? They’re uncertain, unpredictable, and often don’t last.
That man, sitting with his memories, realizes something important. The good things he’s experienced are precious, sure—but they don’t erase the pain he’s felt. The idea that happiness can make up for harm is comforting, but it doesn’t change what’s real. The suffering happened, and no amount of joy can truly cancel it out.
Once you see it this way, the way we measure the value of existence starts to shift. It’s not enough to just hope life will be more good than bad, or to believe happiness can outweigh pain. The harm that comes with existence is real—and it can’t simply be balanced away by later pleasures.
So, the man sits quietly, feeling both gratitude for the joys and sorrow for the hurts. He knows life is always going to be a mix of good and bad, but also that there’s no guarantee the good will ever truly make up for the harm. The limits of compensation become clear. And with that, the way we think about bringing new life into the world changes too.
